assessment.nobel_worthiness: A clean example of quantum mechanics surprising us in a material: the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted flat moire bands at a magic angle, and experiment then found correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene. Theory and measurement fit together quantitatively, and the discovery opened the whole field of moire quantum matter. This is the kind of prediction-then-confirmation story I value.
assessment.attribution: The theory credit is clear (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011); the experimental discovery is credited to Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators (2018). A three-person prize is natural. Others (e.g. Cao, Fatemi, Santos, Kim and co-workers) have claims on the experimental side, and the exact experimental credit within the MIT group could be questioned.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups have reproduced correlated states and superconductivity, and the physics has broadened to twisted TMDs and fractional Chern states. The interpretation of the superconducting pairing is still debated, but the central discovery of flat-band correlated phases is stable. Recognition is timely, perhaps slightly early.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene is not settled.
Fair division of credit between theory and the experimental team, and among experimental contributors, is not fully clear to me.
I rely on memory for dates and details and have not verified them.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the central modern framework for strongly correlated electrons, giving a controlled, quantitative treatment of the Mott transition and, combined with DFT (DFT+DMFT), predictions for real materials such as transition-metal oxides and f-electron systems. Its impact on computational materials theory is large and lasting, and it is directly connected to measured spectra. This is a field I know well.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt (1989) introduced the infinite-dimension limit, Georges and Kotliar (1992) mapped it onto an impurity problem, and the 1996 RMP review with Krauth and Rozenberg consolidated it. The three credited names are a reasonable core, but Walter Metzner and Marcelo Rozenberg are also decisive and are not on the list, so the credit allocation is open.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: decades of use, independent codes, and many comparisons with photoemission and optical data. Reproducibility across implementations is good for the method, though there are known approximation limits (local self-energy). Recognition is overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: Whether a prize for a method (rather than a single physical discovery) fits the will's criterion is a legitimate committee concern.
Omission of Metzner, who is not among the credited names, complicates a fair attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators are a new state of matter, from the Kane-Mele quantum spin Hall prediction through the HgTe quantum well observation and the 3D materials. The topic combines elegant theory with materials-specific predictions and ARPES and transport confirmation. Its influence on condensed-matter physics has been very large.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the Z2 classification and the graphene proposal; Molenkamp led the experimental realization of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe (with theory by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who are not on this list). Hasan's 3D ARPES work is also decisive. Credit is spread over more than three people, so any three-person split is contestable. I prefer Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the cleanest theory-plus-experiment trio from these names.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many groups and materials, with a stable interpretation. Recognition is timely or somewhat late. Practical applications are limited so far, but the discovery is firm.
uncertainties: Credit between 2D quantum spin Hall and 3D topological insulators is contested and a single prize may need to choose one.
Contributions of Bernevig, Zhang, Fu, Hasan and others fall outside or partly outside the credited triad.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Neodymium-iron-boron magnets are the strongest practical permanent magnets, central to wind turbines, electric vehicles and many electronic devices. This links magnetism to sustainable energy, which I care about. The scientific insight (the Nd2Fe14B phase, its anisotropy and magnetic structure) is real and has been confirmed and explained by first-principles theory and neutron diffraction.
assessment.attribution: Sagawa (Sumitomo) and Croat (General Motors) independently announced the material in 1983-84 with different processing routes (sintered versus melt-spun). Both are decisive, so a two-person prize is natural. Priority and patent disputes between the two companies are known, but the scientific credit is reasonably shared.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with four decades of use and a huge literature. Recognition is late but not premature. The committee would need to decide whether this is physics discovery or materials invention; it is arguably an invention in the sense of the will.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views it as sufficiently a physics discovery rather than materials engineering.
The roles of others at the same companies and in the earlier rare-earth magnet work are not fully known to me.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions (1995) and later the giant effect in MgO barriers underlie hard-disk read heads and MRAM, a major spin-dependent quantum transport achievement tied to theoretical band-structure explanations of coherent tunnelling. Importance is high, and the work follows naturally the 2007 GMR prize.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera reported room-temperature TMR independently in 1995; Parkin's group and Yuasa and others demonstrated the giant MgO effect in 2004, with theory by Butler and by Mathon and Umerski. The credited names are a plausible trio, but Yuasa, Djayaprawira and Butler also have decisive claims and are not all listed.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and widely used in technology, with consistent independent confirmations. Timing is late rather than early.
uncertainties: The overlap with the 2007 GMR prize may weigh against it.
Credit for the MgO coherent-tunnelling step involves people not among the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism identifies a third collinear magnetic class with zero net magnetization yet spin-split bands, found through symmetry analysis and first-principles calculations. It is a clear conceptual advance in magnetism, relevant for spintronics, and close to my own field. The theory-to-experiment path (ARPES on MnTe and CrSb) is exactly what I find convincing.
assessment.attribution: Šmejkal, Sinova and Jungwirth are the evident originators of the 2022 classification and the identification as a distinct phase, with earlier related work by Hayami, Yanagi, Kusunose and Yuan et al. that may deserve credit. The credited triad is sensible but the priority question is not settled.
assessment.maturity: Experimental confirmation is recent (2024 onward) and still growing, with several materials and groups. The conceptual picture seems stable, but long-term consequences and applications remain untested. Probably somewhat premature for this cycle.
uncertainties: Priority relative to earlier spin-split antiferromagnet work, including Japanese groups, is a real concern.
Independent confirmation is young; device-relevant effects are still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Angle-resolved photoemission is the key probe for the electronic structure of quantum materials, directly measuring band dispersions, gaps and many-body self-energies in cuprates, topological materials and more. It combines experimental spectroscopy with the theory of the photoemission process, which is the style of science I most admire.
assessment.attribution: The technique itself dates to much earlier work (Plummer, Eberhardt, Spicer, Himpsel and others in the 1970s-80s), while the credited trio are known for high-Tc cuprate applications and instrumentation. Attributing a prize for the technique to these three is difficult, and an application-based prize runs into contested priority.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and universally used, so recognition is not premature, but the discovery framing (technique versus a specific finding) is diffuse.
uncertainties: Credit for the technique versus its application to cuprates is ambiguous.
Prior Nobel-adjacent work in photoemission (Siegbahn's electron spectroscopy) might complicate this.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, now reach roughly 10^-18 fractional uncertainty and make possible tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a future redefinition of the second. This is a precise, reproducible measurement achievement.
assessment.attribution: Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength idea and Ye's implementation of strontium lattice clocks and many-body clock physics are clear and distinct. Hall and Hänsch already received the 2005 prize for the frequency comb; other contributors (e.g. Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley) matter but a two-person prize is workable.
assessment.maturity: Strong independent confirmation across several labs and a clear record of improvement. Timely, though a redefinition of the second has not yet happened. This is outside my main field, so I defer partly to the colleagues on atomic physics.
uncertainties: Outside my core expertise; the relative merits of competing atomic clocks (ion clocks, Al+) are not something I can judge in detail.
Whether the committee would prefer to wait for the redefinition of the second.
